lesson.intro: React is the most requested front-end library in internship and junior web postings. This pack teaches how it really works: components that turn state into UI, JSX as function calls, immutable state updates, keys, forms, effects and data fetching. It ends with how a real project is set up, tested with Vitest and Testing Library, and deployed.
objectives: Build interfaces from components that take props, hold state and compose with children
Predict what a component renders, including conditional JSX, lists with keys and batched state updates
Update arrays and objects in state immutably, and spot bugs such as missing keys, stale closures and effect loops
Fetch data in an effect with loading, error and race-condition handling, and share state by lifting it up or with context
Set up, test and deploy a Vite React project

sections.title: What React solves: components and UI as a function of state
sections.body:
Picture a shopping page. When someone clicks **Add to cart**, the cart badge, the cart drawer, the total and the button label all have to change. With plain DOM code you write each update by hand: find the badge, set its text, find the total, recalculate it, and so on. Every new feature adds another place that can fall out of sync, and the bugs look like a badge that says 3 while the drawer shows 2.

React flips the approach. You describe what the screen should look like **for the current data**, and React works out which DOM changes are needed. People summarize this as **UI = f(state)**: the same data always produces the same screen. When the data changes, React calls your function again, compares the new description with the previous one (this is called **reconciliation**), and updates only the DOM nodes that actually differ.

The unit of reuse is the **component**: a JavaScript function whose name starts with a capital letter and that returns a description of UI, written in JSX. Components nest inside each other to form a tree, just like HTML elements do:

- `App` renders a `Header`, a `ProductList` and a `CartBadge`.
- `ProductList` renders one `ProductCard` per product.
- Data flows **down** the tree as props, and events flow **up** through callback functions. This one-way flow is why you can always find where a value comes from.

A component must be **pure** while it renders: given the same props and state it returns the same JSX, and it does not change variables outside itself, call APIs or touch the DOM during rendering. React may call a component many times, so side effects belong in event handlers or effects, which later sections cover.

React is a library for the view layer, not a full framework. Routing, data fetching and builds come from other tools or from frameworks built on React such as Next.js and React Router. When an internship posting asks for "React experience", it mostly means being comfortable with components, props, state, effects and the tooling around them, which is exactly what this pack covers.
sections.tip: When you design a screen, first ask what data it depends on. The JSX should follow from that data, never the other way around.
sections.pitfall: Doing side effects while rendering, such as fetching or changing a global variable in the component body. React can call a component many times, so render code should only compute and return JSX.

check.question: Your component shows a list of unread messages. A new message arrives and you store it in state. What else must you write to update the screen?
choices: Code that finds the list with document.querySelector and appends the new message
Nothing: React calls the component again with the new state and updates the DOM that changed
A call that tells React to reload the whole page
A loop that rebuilds every list item with innerHTML
check.explanation: Updating state is the whole job. React re-renders the component, compares the new JSX with the old, and patches only the DOM that differs. Touching the DOM by hand fights React and goes stale on the next render.

sections.title: JSX and how it compiles
sections.body:
JSX looks like HTML inside JavaScript, but browsers cannot run it. A build tool (Vite does this for you) turns each tag into a plain function call that creates an object describing the element. This line: `

Hello, {name}!

` becomes, with the modern automatic runtime, `jsxs("h1", { className: "title", children: ["Hello, ", name, "!"] })`. Older setups compiled it to `React.createElement("h1", { className: "title" }, "Hello, ", name, "!")`, which is why old files start with `import React from 'react'`. Either way the result is just an object with a `type` and `props`. Knowing that explains most of JSX's rules: - **Curly braces hold expressions**, anything that produces a value: `{user.name}`, `{items.length * 2}`, `{isOpen ? 'Close' : 'Open'}`. Statements such as `if` and `for` cannot go inside, because they are not values. Use a ternary or `&&`, or compute a variable above the `return`. - **One root per return.** A function returns one value, so two sibling tags must be wrapped, either in a `
` or in a **fragment** `<>...`, which adds nothing to the DOM. - **Attributes use JavaScript property names.** `class` is `className`, `for` is `htmlFor`, and multi-word attributes are camelCase: `onClick`, `tabIndex`. `style` takes an object: `style={{ fontSize: 18 }}`. `aria-*` and `data-*` keep their dashes. - **Every tag closes**: ``, ``, `
`. - **Capitalization decides the type.** `
` compiles to the string `'div'`; `` compiles to the variable `Card`, your component. That is why component names must start with a capital letter. - **What renders**: strings and numbers render as text. `null`, `undefined`, `true` and `false` render nothing, which makes `{isAdmin && }` work. The number `0` is not on that list, so `{count && }` shows a stray 0 when count is 0. Write `{count > 0 && }`. Text in braces is escaped automatically, so rendering user input with `{comment}` cannot inject HTML. That is one reason React apps are less prone to cross-site scripting.
sections.pitfall: `{count && <Badge />}` renders a literal 0 when count is 0, because 0 is a number and numbers render. Compare explicitly: `{count > 0 && <Badge />}`.

activity.title: Build JSX by hand
activity.prompt: This is a tiny model of what JSX compiles to: `h()` only builds plain objects, and `render()` turns them into HTML text the way React turns them into DOM. Run it and find the stray 0. Then fix the condition the way you would in real JSX and run it again.

props.task:
Change the condition so a count of 0 renders nothing. The last line should become `
Inbox
`. Then try count = 3 for fun.

check.question: Which of these can go inside curly braces in JSX?
choices: An if statement
A for loop
A ternary such as {isOpen ? 'Close' : 'Open'}
A const declaration
check.explanation: Braces hold expressions, things that produce a value, because JSX compiles to function arguments. if, for and const are statements; use a ternary, &&, map, or compute a variable above the return.

sections.title: Props and composition
sections.body:
Components take inputs called **props**, short for properties. In JSX they look like attributes; inside the component they arrive as one object, which you usually destructure in the parameter list:

`function Avatar({ user, size = 48 }) { ... }`

`size = 48` is a default, used when the parent does not pass `size`. Props can be any JavaScript value: strings, numbers, arrays, objects, other JSX and functions. Strings can be quoted (`name="Ana"`); everything else goes in braces (`size={64}`, `user={currentUser}`, `onSelect={handleSelect}`).

Props are **read-only**. A component must never change its props, just as a pure function does not change its arguments. If something needs to change over time, it is state (next section), owned by some component that passes it down.

**Composition** is how React builds big interfaces from small parts. The special prop `children` holds whatever JSX the parent puts between the opening and closing tags. A `Card` that renders `{children}` inside a styled box can wrap a profile, a form or a chart without knowing anything about them. This replaces most of what other frameworks do with inheritance: React code almost never says `class Card extends Box`. Instead, specialized components render general ones with particular props.

Functions passed as props are how children talk to parents. The parent owns the data and passes both the value and a callback, for example `<ProductCard product={p} onAdd={addToCart} />`. The child calls `onAdd(product.id)` when its button is clicked. By convention, callback props start with `on` and the parent's handler functions start with `handle`.

When should you split a component? A good rule from the React docs is single responsibility: if a piece of UI has its own job, or a component grows past a screenful of JSX, extract it. Do not define a component inside another component's body, though. It is recreated on every render, React sees a brand new component type each time, and its state resets.
sections.tip: Read a component's parameter list first. It tells you everything the component depends on from outside.
sections.pitfall: Changing a prop inside a child, for example `items.sort()` on an array prop. `sort` reorders the parent's array in place, behind React's back. Copy first: `[...items].sort()` or `items.toSorted()`.

check.question: A `ProductCard` needs to tell its parent that the user clicked Add, and the cart state lives in the parent. What is the React way?
choices: The card changes one of its props, and React tells the parent
The card imports the parent's state setter and calls it
The card fires a DOM event that React copies into the parent's state
The parent passes a callback prop such as onAdd, and the card calls it
check.explanation: Data flows down as props and events flow up through callbacks. The parent owns the state and passes a function; the child calls it with whatever the parent needs, such as the product id.

sections.title: State with useState, and why updates are immutable
sections.body:
Props come from the parent. **State** is data a component owns and changes over time: the text in a search box, whether a menu is open, the items in a cart. You add it with the `useState` hook:

`const [count, setCount] = useState(0)`

`useState(0)` returns the current value and a setter. Calling `setCount(5)` does not change the `count` variable in the code that is running. It asks React to **re-render**: React calls your component again, and in that new call `useState` returns 5. Each render sees a fixed snapshot of state, which is why `console.log(count)` right after `setCount(count + 1)` still prints the old value.

React also **batches** updates made in the same event: it runs your whole handler first, then re-renders once. So three calls to `setCount(count + 1)` in one click all compute 0 + 1, and the result is 1, not 3. When the next value depends on the previous one, pass an **updater function**: `setCount(c => c + 1)`. React queues updaters and runs them in order, each receiving the result of the one before.

**Treat state as immutable.** React decides whether anything changed by comparing the old and new value with `Object.is`. For an array or object that compares references, not contents. If you `push` onto the existing array and pass the same array back, React sees the same reference and skips the re-render, and your screen goes stale. Always create a new value:

- Add: `setItems([...items, newItem])`
- Remove: `setItems(items.filter(i => i.id !== id))`
- Update one: `setItems(items.map(i => i.id === id ? { ...i, done: true } : i))`
- Change a field: `setUser({ ...user, name: 'Ana' })`

Spread copies only one level deep, so a nested object needs its own spread at each level you change. Immutable updates also make undo and change detection cheap, because old versions are never overwritten.

Hooks follow two **Rules of Hooks**: call them only at the top level of a component or custom hook (never inside `if`, loops, nested functions or after an early `return`), and only from React functions. React matches hooks to their state by call order, so a hook that runs in one render but not the next shifts every hook after it.
sections.tip: If the new value depends on the old one, use the updater form: `setCount(c => c + 1)`.
sections.pitfall: Mutating state and then setting it: `items.push(x); setItems(items)`. The reference is unchanged, so React skips the update. Build a new array or object every time.

activity.title: Same reference, no re-render
activity.prompt: React compares old and new state with `Object.is`. Run this to see which updates React would notice. Then fix the toggle so todo 1 becomes done in a new object while the original stays untouched.

props.task: Fix the `toggled` line with spread syntax. The last two lines should both print true.
props.expectOutput:
push then set: false
spread: true
new array: true
todo 1 is done: true
original untouched: true

check.question: A click handler calls `setCount(5)`. When does `count` become 5?
choices: Immediately, on the next line of the handler
In the next render, when useState returns 5
Only after the page reloads
Never, unless you also assign count = 5
check.explanation: The setter schedules a re-render. The running handler keeps its snapshot of count; the next call of the component gets 5 from useState.

sections.title: Rendering lists with keys
sections.body:
Lists come from arrays, and you turn an array of data into an array of elements with `map`:

`{products.map(p => <ProductCard key={p.id} product={p} />)}`

To show only some items, chain `filter` first: `products.filter(p => p.inStock).map(...)`. JSX renders an array of elements just fine.

The `key` tells React **which item is which** between renders. When the list changes, React matches old and new children by key. Same key: same component instance, so its state and DOM node are kept and only its props update. A new key mounts a new component, and a key that disappears unmounts one.

Without keys, React falls back to position and logs a warning: `Each child in a list should have a unique "key" prop.` Using the array **index** as the key silences the warning but keeps the position problem. Picture a shopping list where each row has a text input. You type a note into the first row, Milk, then add Bread at the top. With index keys, Bread is now index 0, so it inherits row 0's component, including the note you typed for Milk. With `key={item.id}`, the note stays with Milk. Index keys are fine only for lists that never reorder, filter or insert anywhere but the end.

Good keys are:

- **Unique among siblings.** Two different lists can reuse the same keys.
- **Stable.** The same item gets the same key on every render. Database ids, slugs and ids created once when the item is created all work. Never generate keys during render with `Math.random()` or `crypto.randomUUID()`: every render would remount every row, losing state and focus.

The key goes on the outermost element returned from `map`. If you return a fragment, use the long form, `<Fragment key={term.id}>`, because the `<>` shorthand cannot take attributes. Keys are not passed to your component as a prop; if the child needs the id, pass it separately.

Keys have a second use: changing a component's key on purpose tells React to throw away its state and start fresh. `<ProfileForm key={userId} />` resets the form whenever you switch users.
sections.pitfall: Using the index as the key for a list that can reorder, filter or grow at the front. Row state then sticks to positions instead of items. Use a stable id from the data.

check.question: Users can sort and filter a list rendered with `users.map(...)`. Which key should each row use?
choices: user.id from the database
The array index
Math.random()
user.name, which two users may share
check.explanation: A key must be unique among siblings and stable across renders. An id from the data is both. Indexes change when the list is sorted or filtered, random keys change every render, and names can repeat.

sections.title: Events and controlled form inputs
sections.body:
Event handlers are props whose names start with `on`: `onClick`, `onChange`, `onSubmit`, `onKeyDown`. You pass a **function**, and React calls it when the event fires:

- `onClick={handleSave}` passes the function. Correct.
- `onClick={handleSave()}` calls it **during render** and passes its return value. If it sets state, React re-renders, calls it again, and stops with `Too many re-renders`.
- `onClick={() => removeItem(item.id)}` wraps a call that needs arguments in an arrow function. Correct.

The handler receives an event object (React's wrapper around the browser event) with the usual `e.target`, `e.preventDefault()` and `e.stopPropagation()`.

Forms in React are usually **controlled**: the input's value lives in state, and every keystroke goes through your code:

`<input value={email} onChange={e => setEmail(e.target.value)} />`

React sets the input from state, and `onChange` updates state, so state is the **single source of truth**. That makes validating, formatting and clearing the form trivial. If you set `value` and forget `onChange`, the input is read-only and React warns you. Checkboxes use `checked` and `e.target.checked` instead. An **uncontrolled** input (`defaultValue`, read later through a ref or `FormData`) is fine for simple forms but gives you less control.

For a form with several fields, one state object plus each input's `name` keeps the handler short: `setForm({ ...form, [e.target.name]: e.target.value })`. The square brackets make a computed property name.

Submit with `<form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>` and a `type="submit"` button, which also makes the Enter key work. Call `e.preventDefault()` first: otherwise the browser does its own form submission and reloads the page, wiping your app's state.

Do not store what you can compute. Whether the form is valid, how many characters are left, or a filtered list are **derived values**: compute them during render from the state you already have. Keeping them in extra state creates two sources of truth that drift apart.
sections.pitfall: Writing `onClick={handleClick()}`. The parentheses call the function while rendering. Pass the function itself, or wrap calls that need arguments: `onClick={() => handleClick(id)}`.

check.question: An input has `value={name}` but no `onChange`. What happens when the user types?
choices: The text appears and name updates automatically
The text appears, but name keeps its old value
The box does not change, and React warns that the field is read-only
React throws an error and the form unmounts
check.explanation: A controlled input always shows the state value. With no onChange, nothing updates state, so every keystroke is undone on the spot. React's console warning suggests adding onChange or using defaultValue.

sections.title: Effects with useEffect, and when not to use one
sections.body:
Rendering must be pure, but apps also talk to things outside React: start a timer, subscribe to a WebSocket, update `document.title`, connect to a chat room. **Effects** synchronize a component with an external system. `useEffect(setup, dependencies)` runs `setup` after React has updated the screen.

The **dependency array** says when to run it again:

- No array: after every render. Rarely what you want.
- `[]`: once, after the component first appears (mounts).
- `[roomId]`: after the first render, and again whenever `roomId` changes, compared with `Object.is`.

The setup can return a **cleanup** function. React runs it before running the effect again with new dependencies, and when the component unmounts. When `roomId` changes from `a` to `b`, the order is: render with `b`, update the DOM, cleanup disconnects from `a`, setup connects to `b`. Every subscription, timer or listener you start needs a matching cleanup, or it leaks. In development, **Strict Mode** deliberately runs setup, cleanup, setup when a component mounts, so a missing cleanup shows up right away as a double connection. Production runs it once.

Three classic effect bugs:

- **Infinite loop.** An effect with no array that sets state causes a re-render, which runs the effect again, forever. The same happens when an effect sets a value it also depends on, or depends on an object or function that is created fresh on every render.
- **Stale closure.** An interval created in an effect with `[]` captures `seconds` from the first render. `setSeconds(seconds + 1)` then always computes 0 + 1, so the clock sticks at 1. Use the updater form, `setSeconds(s => s + 1)`.
- **Lying about dependencies.** Leaving a value out of the array to stop re-runs leads to stale data. The `react-hooks/exhaustive-deps` lint rule catches this, so keep it on.

**You might not need an effect.** If you can compute something from props and state, compute it during render (`const fullName = first + ' ' + last`) instead of copying it into more state with an effect. If something should happen because the user clicked, do it in the click handler. To reset state when a prop changes, change the component's `key`. Effects are for external systems; most other uses add an extra render and a chance for bugs.
sections.pitfall: Setting state inside an effect that has no dependency array, or that depends on the value it sets. Each update triggers a render, which triggers the effect again. Give the effect the right dependencies, or move the logic out of the effect.

check.question: Which of these actually needs an effect?
choices: Computing a cart total from the items in state
Sending a form to the server when the user clicks Submit
Filtering a list by the text in a search box
Subscribing to a WebSocket while a chat component is on screen
check.explanation: A WebSocket is an external system that must be connected while the component is shown and disconnected afterwards, which is exactly what an effect with cleanup does. Totals and filters are derived during render, and a submit belongs in the event handler.

sections.title: Fetching data with loading and error states
sections.body:
Fetching is the effect you will write most, and interviewers like to see it done carefully. A request has three outcomes your UI must handle: still **loading**, failed with an **error**, or succeeded with **data**. Model all three in state and render a branch for each.

Walk through the code below:

- The effect depends on `[userId]`, so it fetches when the component mounts and again whenever the user changes.
- It resets `loading` and `error` before starting, so a new request does not show the previous error.
- `fetch` rejects only on network failures. A 404 or 500 still resolves, with `res.ok` set to false, so you check `res.ok` and throw yourself.
- The `ignore` flag handles a **race condition**. Click user 1, then quickly user 2. If the response for user 1 arrives last, it would overwrite user 2's data and the page would show the wrong person. Cleanup runs when `userId` changes and sets `ignore = true` for the old request, so its late response is dropped. An `AbortController` does the same job and also cancels the network request.
- The render checks error first, then loading, then shows the data.

In a real project you would often use a data library such as **TanStack Query** or **SWR**, or the loader of a framework. They add caching, de-duplication, retries and refetching when the window regains focus, and they hide this boilerplate. Learn the manual version anyway: it is a common interview exercise, and it explains what those libraries do for you.

Two more habits make the difference between a demo and a real app. Show something useful while loading, such as a skeleton or a spinner, and give errors a way forward, such as a Retry button. And keep the API's base URL in configuration (in Vite, `import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL`) instead of scattering hard-coded URLs through your components.
sections.pitfall: Assuming `fetch` rejects on HTTP errors. A 404 or 500 resolves normally; check `res.ok` and throw, or your code will try to render an error response as if it were data.

activity.title: Reproduce the race
activity.prompt: Two requests race: user 1 is slow, user 2 is fast. The cleanup for user 1 has already run, yet its late response still wins. Use the `ignore` flag to drop it.

props.task: Guard the update with the ignore flag so the final line says Ben.
props.expectOutput:
request for user 1 started
request for user 2 started
final screen: Ben

check.question: The user switches from profile 1 to profile 2 quickly, and the response for profile 1 arrives last. Without an ignore flag or AbortController, what does the page show?
choices: Profile 2, because React cancels old requests automatically
Profile 1, even though profile 2 is selected
An error, because two requests cannot run at once
Nothing, because both responses are discarded
check.explanation: Each response calls setUser when it arrives, so the last one to arrive wins, and that is the stale profile 1. Cleanup that sets ignore = true (or aborts the request) stops old responses from updating state.

sections.title: Lifting state up, context and reducers
sections.body:
Sometimes two components need the same state. A `SearchBar` holds the query text, and a `ProductTable` needs that query to filter its rows. They are siblings, so neither can read the other's state. The fix is **lifting state up**: move the state to their closest common parent, pass the value down to both as props, and pass the setter (or a callback) to the one that changes it. Now there is one source of truth, and both stay in sync. This is the most common refactor in React; the "Thinking in React" tutorial in the official docs builds a whole app around it.

Lifting can lead to **prop drilling**: passing a prop through several components that do not use it, only so a deeply nested child can. For data that many components at different depths need, such as the theme, the signed-in user or the language, use **context**:

- **Create** it once: `const ThemeContext = createContext('light')`. The argument is the default value, used when no provider is above the reader.
- **Provide** it high in the tree: `<ThemeContext value={theme}>...</ThemeContext>`. Since React 19 the context itself works as the provider; older code writes `<ThemeContext.Provider value={theme}>`, which still works.
- **Read** it anywhere below: `const theme = useContext(ThemeContext)`.

Every component that reads a context re-renders when its value changes, so context is not a replacement for all props or a store for fast-changing data. Use it for broad, slow-changing values, and keep passing props for the rest.

When state updates get complicated (many fields, many ways to change them), move the logic into a **reducer** with `useReducer`. A reducer is a pure function `(state, action) => newState`. Components call `dispatch({ type: 'added', id })` to describe what happened, and the reducer decides how state changes. Reducers are easy to test because they are plain functions, and the immutable update rules still apply: return a new value, never modify the old one. A reducer combined with context is a common way to share app state without an extra library; larger apps may add Redux Toolkit or Zustand.
sections.pitfall: Copying a prop into state, such as `useState(props.query)`, so that two components each hold "the same" value. The copies drift apart. Keep one owner and pass the value down.

activity.title: Write a reducer
activity.prompt: `useReducer` applies each dispatched action to the current state with your reducer, just like `reduce` does here. Finish the `removed` case without mutating the cart.

props.task: Make `removed` return a new array without the line for `action.id`. Only apples should be left.

check.question: A `Filters` panel and a `ResultsList` are siblings, and both need the selected category. Where should the category state live?
choices: In their closest common parent, passed down as props
In Filters, with ResultsList reading it through a ref
In both components, kept in sync with an effect
In a global variable outside React
check.explanation: Lifting the state to the closest common parent gives one source of truth: the parent passes the value to both and the setter to Filters. Two copies kept in sync with effects drift and cost extra renders.

sections.title: How a real React project is set up, tested and deployed
sections.body:
Most new React single-page apps start from a **Vite** template: `npm create vite@latest my-app -- --template react` (or `react-ts` for TypeScript), then `cd my-app`, `npm install` and `npm run dev`. If you need server rendering and routing built in, the React docs suggest a framework such as Next.js or React Router instead. Either way, the layout looks much like this:

- `index.html`: the single HTML page, with an empty `<div id="root">`.
- `src/main.jsx`: the entry point. `createRoot(document.getElementById('root')).render(<App />)` hands that div to React.
- `src/App.jsx` and `src/components/`: your components, one per file, named in PascalCase. Tests often sit next to them, as in `Counter.test.jsx`.
- `public/`: files copied as they are, such as `favicon.svg` and `robots.txt`.
- `package.json`: dependencies and **npm scripts**. `npm run dev` starts the dev server with hot reload, `npm run build` writes an optimized production bundle to `dist/`, `npm run preview` serves that bundle locally, and you add `test` and `lint` scripts.

**Configuration** comes from `.env` files. Vite exposes only variables whose names start with `VITE_`, read as `import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL`. They are baked into the bundle at build time, so anyone can read them in the browser: never put a secret there. Secrets stay on a server.

**Testing** uses **Vitest**, a Jest-compatible runner that shares Vite's config (set `test: { environment: 'jsdom' }`), with **React Testing Library**. Testing Library renders a component into a simulated DOM and pushes you to test like a user: find elements by role and accessible name, click and type with `user-event`, and check what is visible. Prefer `getByRole('button', { name: /add/i })` over class names or test ids, because it also fails when real users, including screen reader users, would struggle. Test behavior, not internal state.

**Deploying** a Vite app means deploying static files. `npm run build` produces HTML, JavaScript and CSS in `dist/` that any static host can serve: Netlify, Vercel, Cloudflare Pages or GitHub Pages. Connect the repository, set the build command to `npm run build` and the publish directory to `dist`, and every push to `main` deploys. One catch: with client-side routing, refreshing on `/settings` asks the server for a file that does not exist. Add a rewrite that serves `index.html` for every path (on Netlify, a `_redirects` file with `/* /index.html 200`). The Shipping Code pack covers CI and hosting in depth.
sections.tip: Run `npm run build && npm run preview` before you deploy. It catches problems that only show up in the production bundle, such as a missing environment variable.

activity.title: Read a package.json
activity.prompt: This is a typical package.json for a Vite React app. Before the quiz, find the script that produces `dist/`, the test runner, and which packages ship to users (dependencies) versus tools used only while developing (devDependencies).

check.question: What does `npm run build` produce for a Vite React app, and where can it run?
choices: A Node server in build/ that must run on a virtual machine
A Docker image that is pushed to Docker Hub
Static HTML, JavaScript and CSS in dist/, which any static host can serve
Only source maps, because the host compiles JSX itself
check.explanation: A client-rendered React app compiles down to static files. Netlify, Vercel, Cloudflare Pages or GitHub Pages can serve dist/ directly; no server process is needed unless you add one.

keyTerms.definition: A function, named in PascalCase, that returns JSX describing part of the UI for its props and state.
HTML-like syntax that compiles to function calls creating element objects.
Read-only inputs a parent passes to a component, including children and callbacks.
Data a component owns and changes over time with a setter, which triggers a re-render.
React calling a component again after state changes, then updating only the DOM that differs.
Replacing an array or object in state with a new one instead of changing it in place.
A stable, unique id on list items that tells React which item is which between renders.
A form field whose value comes from state and changes only through onChange.
Code in useEffect that synchronizes a component with an external system after rendering.
The list of values that decides when an effect runs again.
A way to pass a value to every component below a provider without prop drilling.
A pure function (state, action) => next state, used with useReducer.

summary: A component is a function that returns JSX for its props and state; React re-renders it when state changes and updates only the DOM that differs.
JSX compiles to function calls that build plain objects, so braces hold expressions, a return needs one root and attributes use JavaScript names.
State is a snapshot per render: use updater functions for chained updates and always replace arrays and objects instead of mutating them.
Give list items stable, unique keys from your data, never random values, and never indexes for lists that reorder.
Use effects only to sync with external systems, with correct dependencies and cleanup; derive everything else during render.
Lift shared state to the closest common parent, use context for broad values, and ship with Vite, Vitest, Testing Library and a static host.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend who knows JavaScript what happens when they click a React button that calls setCount: why the screen updates, why count still holds the old value inside the handler, and why pushing onto an array in state does not update the screen.

questions.question: What does a React function component return?
choices: A list of DOM operations for React to run in order
An HTML string that React inserts with innerHTML
A description of the UI, written as JSX, for the current props and state
A CSS class that React applies to the root element
questions.explanation: A component returns JSX, which is a description of what the UI should look like. React compares it with the previous description and applies only the needed DOM changes. Components do not return DOM operations or HTML strings.

questions.question: What does "UI is a function of state" mean in React, and why does it cut down on bugs?
questions.answer: You describe what the screen should look like for the current data, and React re-renders and updates the DOM whenever that data changes. Because the screen is always computed from one source of data, parts of the page cannot drift out of sync the way hand-written DOM updates can.
questions.explanation: Hand-written DOM updates must be repeated everywhere the data appears, and missing one leaves the page inconsistent. Deriving the screen from state removes that whole class of bugs.
questions.concept: UI as a function of state

questions.question: A teammate writes a component named `profileCard` and renders it as `<profileCard />`. What happens?
choices: It works exactly like <ProfileCard />
React creates an unknown <profilecard> HTML element instead of calling the function
The build fails with a syntax error
React calls the function but ignores its props
questions.explanation: Lowercase JSX tags compile to strings, so React creates a DOM element called profilecard and never calls the function. React also warns about the casing. Rename it ProfileCard.

questions.question: What does this component render when `count` is 0?
choices: 0
New messages
Nothing: the component returns null
questions.explanation: `0 && ...` evaluates to 0, and React renders numbers as text, so the div contains 0. false, null and undefined would render nothing. Write `count > 0 && ...`.

questions.question:
With the classic JSX transform, what does `

Hi, {name}

` compile to?
choices: document.createElement("h1", { className: "title" })

React.render("

Hi, " + name + "

")
new HTMLHeadingElement({ className: "title", children: name })
React.createElement("h1", { className: "title" }, "Hi, ", name)
questions.explanation: Each tag becomes a call that creates an element object: the type, a props object, then the children. The modern automatic runtime calls jsx() from react/jsx-runtime instead, with children inside props, but the idea is the same.

questions.question: This component does not compile. What is wrong?
choices: The nav element cannot be used inside a component
It returns two sibling elements; wrap them in a fragment <>...</> or a div
h1 must be written as a self-closing tag in JSX
JSX cannot be wrapped in parentheses after return
questions.explanation: A component returns one value, and two sibling tags would be two values. Wrap them in a fragment, `<>...</>`, which adds no extra DOM node, or in a real element such as a div.

questions.question: Which of these JSX snippets compile and work in React? Select all that apply.
choices: Error
<button onClick={save}>Save</button>

{if (open)
  • Item
    • }
<input type="text">
Error
questions.explanation: The image is closed, style gets an object and onClick gets a function. An if statement is not an expression, so it cannot go in braces. Every tag must close, so `<input type="text">` is a syntax error. A style string compiles but React throws at runtime because style needs an object.

questions.question: What does `page` render?
choices: Hello, ! and Hello, Ana!
Hello, undefined! and Hello, Ana!
Hello, friend! and Hello, Ana!
Hello, friend! twice, because the default wins
questions.explanation: A destructuring default applies only when the prop is missing (undefined). The first Greeting passes no name, so it uses friend; the second passes Ana.

questions.question: Fill the blank so `Panel` displays whatever the parent puts between `<Panel>` and `</Panel>`.
choices: content
props
inner
children
questions.explanation: Nested JSX arrives in the children prop. Destructure it next to title and render it where the content should go.

questions.question: After this component renders, the parent's own list of names later shows up sorted too, although nobody sorted it there. Why?
choices: sort() reorders the parent's array in place; use [...names].sort() or names.toSorted()
The key prop sorts the parent's data to match
map() mutates the array it is called on
React copies props deeply, so the parent cannot be affected
questions.explanation: Array.prototype.sort sorts in place and returns the same array, so it changed the parent's data behind React's back. Copy before sorting, or use toSorted, which returns a new array.

questions.question: `count` starts at 0. What does the button show after one click?
questions.explanation: All three calls read the same snapshot, count = 0, so each one sets 1. React batches them into one re-render with count = 1. Use setCount(c => c + 1) to add 3.

questions.question: Fill the blank so one click adds exactly 3 to `count`.
choices: count + 1
count++
() => count + 1
questions.explanation: An updater receives the latest queued value, so three updaters chain 0 to 1 to 2 to 3. count + 1 reads the stale snapshot three times. count++ tries to reassign a const. () => count + 1 ignores the previous value, so it also ends at 1.

questions.question: Clicking Add does not update the list on screen. What is wrong?
choices: Date.now() cannot be used as an id
setTodos must be called before push
useState can only hold primitive values, not arrays
push mutates the same array, so React sees the same reference and skips the re-render
questions.explanation: push changes the existing array, so setTodos receives the very same reference. React compares with Object.is, sees no change and skips the re-render. Use setTodos([...todos, newTodo]).

questions.question: What does the first click log?
choices: undefined
Nothing, because the component re-renders first
questions.explanation: Setting state schedules a re-render; it does not change the count variable in the handler that is already running. The handler logs 0, and the next render sees 1.

questions.question: `todos` is an array in state. Which calls make a correct, immutable update? Select all that apply.
choices: setTodos([...todos, newTodo])
setTodos(todos.filter((t) => t.id !== id))
setTodos(todos.map((t) => (t.id === id ? { ...t, done: true } : t)))
todos[0].done = true; setTodos([...todos])
setTodos(todos.reverse())
questions.explanation: Spread, filter and map all build new arrays, and the map version also copies the changed todo. Assigning todos[0].done mutates an object that the old state still shares. reverse() reorders in place and returns the same array, so React sees no change.

questions.question: Profile renders fine for a signed-out visitor, then crashes with "Rendered more hooks than during the previous render" when the user signs in. Why?
choices: useState cannot hold strings
The second useState runs only after the early return check, so the number of hooks changes between renders
Components are not allowed to return early
Two useState calls in one component are not allowed
questions.explanation: React matches hooks by call order. Signed out, only one hook runs before the early return; signed in, two run. Call every hook at the top level, before any early return.

questions.question: `n` starts at 5. A click handler runs `setN(n + 1)` and then `setN((n) => n * 2)`. What is `n` after the re-render?
questions.explanation: React processes the queue in order: setN(n + 1) replaces the value with 6, then the updater doubles it to 12.

questions.question: React logs a warning for this component. What is the fix?
choices: Wrap the map call in a fragment
Replace map with forEach
Give each li a stable key, such as key={p.id}
Give the ul an id attribute
questions.explanation: Elements built with map need a key so React can tell the items apart between renders. A stable id from the data is the right choice.

questions.question: A todo list renders `<TodoRow key={index} todo={todo} />`, and each row keeps its own `isEditing` state. You click Edit on the first row, then delete the first todo. What happens?
choices: No row is in edit mode, because the edited todo is gone
React throws a duplicate key error
Every row switches into edit mode
The todo that moves into the first row now shows in edit mode
questions.explanation: With index keys, the row component at index 0 survives the delete and simply gets the next todo as props, so its isEditing state now applies to the wrong todo. key={todo.id} would unmount the deleted row's component.

questions.question: Each glossary term renders a `<dt>` and a `<dd>` with no wrapper element. Where does the key go?
choices: On a <Fragment key={term.id}> wrapping both
On the <dt> only
On both the dt and the dd, with the same value
On the parent <dl>
questions.explanation: The key belongs on the outermost thing map returns. Here that is a fragment, and only the long form Fragment can take a key.

questions.question: As soon as the list renders, every item deletes itself without any clicks. Why?
choices: onDelete(id) runs during render; pass a function instead: onClick={() => onDelete(id)}
Buttons fire onClick once when they first mount
The id must be converted to a string first
onDelete must be bound to this in a constructor
questions.explanation: onDelete(id) runs while rendering, and its return value is passed to onClick. Each call removes an item from the parent's state, so the whole list empties itself. Pass a function: onClick={() => onDelete(id)}.

questions.question: Fill the blank to make this a working controlled input.
questions.code:
const [query, setQuery] = useState('')

return <input value={query} onChange={(e) => setQuery(_____)} />
choices: e.value
e.target.value
query + e.key
e.target.checked
questions.explanation: onChange receives an event whose target is the input element, and its value property holds the current text. checked is for checkboxes.

questions.question: One handler serves every input in the form, and each input has a `name` attribute matching a field. Fill the blank.
choices: e.target.name
name
form[e.target.name]
[e.target.name]
questions.explanation: Square brackets make a computed key, so the field named by the input is the one replaced. Without brackets, e.target.name is a syntax error as a key, and name would create a literal field called name.

questions.question: Match each effect setup to when React runs it.

pairs.right: After the first render and whenever userId changes
Before the next run and when the component unmounts

questions.explanation: The dependency array controls re-runs: none means every render, empty means only after mount, and listed values re-run it when they change. The returned cleanup runs before each re-run and on unmount.

questions.question: The network tab shows /api/products being requested over and over. Why?
choices: fetch retries automatically until it gets an empty response
setProducts must be called before fetch
The effect has no dependency array, so every setProducts re-render runs it again; add []
ProductGrid re-runs its parent's effects whenever it renders
questions.explanation: With no dependency array the effect runs after every render. Each response calls setProducts with a new array, which re-renders, which runs the effect again. Add [] so it fetches once.

questions.question: The stopwatch shows 1 and then never changes. What is the fix?
choices: Remove the cleanup so the interval keeps running
Use setSeconds((s) => s + 1), because the interval's closure always sees seconds = 0
Use a 100 ms interval so React notices the changes
Move the useState call inside the effect
questions.explanation: The interval callback was created during the first render, so it always sees seconds = 0 and keeps setting 1. The updater form reads the latest value each time.

questions.question: What is the best way to improve this code?
choices: Add fullName to the dependency array
Switch to useLayoutEffect so the name appears sooner
Store fullName in a ref instead of state
Remove the fullName state and effect, and compute const fullName = first + ' ' + last during render
questions.explanation: fullName can be computed from first and last on every render. The effect version stores a duplicate, renders once with a stale empty value, then renders again.
questions.concept: you might not need an effect

questions.question: A ChatRoom's effect depends on `[roomId]`. It mounts with room a, then roomId changes to b, then the component unmounts. Put what happens in order.
items: Unmount: cleanup disconnects from room b
questions.explanation: Effects run after rendering. When a dependency changes, React renders with the new value, then cleans up the old effect before running the new one. Unmounting runs the last cleanup.

questions.question: In development, a ChatRoom's effect logs connect, disconnect, connect when it first appears. In production it logs connect once. Why?
choices: Strict Mode runs setup, cleanup and setup again on mount in development to expose missing cleanup
The effect has a bug that only the production build fixes
Development builds keep two copies of every component on the page
The dependency array is ignored in development
questions.explanation: Strict Mode remounts components once in development so that effects without proper cleanup are easy to spot. It has no effect on production builds.

questions.question: `fetch('/api/users/999')` gets a 404 Not Found response. What does the promise do?
choices: It rejects with a NotFoundError
It resolves with null
It resolves with a Response whose ok is false, so you must check res.ok and throw
It retries until the server returns 200
questions.explanation: fetch rejects only when the request cannot complete, such as a network failure. HTTP error statuses resolve normally with ok set to false, so check res.ok and throw.

questions.question: Fill the blank so a response for an old userId cannot overwrite newer data.
choices: ignore = true
ignore = false
setUser(null)
fetchUser.cancel()
questions.explanation: Cleanup runs when userId changes. Setting ignore to true marks the old request as stale, so its late response is dropped. Clearing the user would flash empty data but still let the stale response win.

questions.question: Name the three states a data-fetching component should handle, and what it shows in each.
questions.answer: Loading: a spinner or skeleton while waiting. Error: a message, ideally with a way to retry. Success: the data itself, plus an empty state if the data is an empty list.
questions.explanation: Users notice when a page shows nothing while loading or silently fails. Handling all three states, plus empty results, is what interviewers look for.

questions.question: The signed-in user is needed by a header, a sidebar and a settings page several levels below App, and the components in between only pass it along. What fits best?
choices: Copy the user into state in every component that needs it
Provide the user through a context and read it with useContext where needed
Store the user in a module-level variable and read it directly
Pass the user to each component as its key prop
questions.explanation: Context lets any component below the provider read the value directly, so the components in between no longer pass a prop they do not use. Copies in local state drift apart, and a module variable does not re-render anything when it changes.

questions.question: What does App render?
choices: dark, then dark
light, then light
undefined, then dark
light, then dark
questions.explanation: useContext returns the value of the nearest provider above the component. The first Label has none, so it gets the default from createContext. The second is inside a provider with value dark.

questions.question: What does this log?
questions.explanation: Starting at 10: add 5 gives 15, add 2 gives 17, reset gives 0, add 4 gives 4. useReducer applies dispatched actions the same way, one at a time.

questions.question: Type the npm command that runs a Vite project's production build, which writes the bundle to dist/.
questions.explanation: npm run executes a script from package.json, and the build script runs vite build. npm run dev starts the development server instead.

questions.question: Match each part of a Vite React project to its job.

pairs.right: The single page, with an empty root div
Build output you upload to a static host
Files copied as they are, such as favicon.svg

questions.explanation: index.html loads main.jsx, which renders App into the root div. public files are copied as they are, the build writes dist, and package.json holds the dependencies and scripts.

questions.question: A Vite app needs the API's base URL. Which approach is right?
choices: Set VITE_API_URL in .env and read import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL, knowing it is visible in the bundle
Set API_URL in .env and read process.env.API_URL in the browser
Put the API's secret key in VITE_API_KEY, since Vite encrypts it
Hard-code the URL in every component that calls the API
questions.explanation: Vite exposes only VITE_ variables to client code, through import.meta.env, and bakes them into the bundle where anyone can read them. process.env does not exist in the browser, and no bundler can hide a secret that ships to users.

questions.question: A Testing Library test needs to click the Add to cart button. Which query follows the library's guidance best?
choices: container.querySelector('.btn-primary')
screen.getByTestId('add-btn')
screen.getByRole('button', { name: /add to cart/i })
container.firstChild.lastChild
questions.explanation: Queries by role and accessible name find elements the way users and assistive technology do, and they survive styling changes. Class selectors and DOM paths break on refactors, and test ids are a last resort.

questions.question: Your Vite app uses client-side routing. It works when you start from the home page, but refreshing on /settings shows the host's 404 page. What fixes it?
choices: Renaming dist to build
A rewrite that serves index.html for every path, such as /* /index.html 200 on Netlify
Adding a key prop to the router
Running npm run dev on the production server
questions.explanation: The host looks for a file called settings, which does not exist. A rewrite that serves index.html for every path lets the app load and the client-side router show the right page.
